# Popliteal (Baker) cyst

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Joint diseases > Popliteal (Baker) cyst*

[Original Article Link](/library/UF0bh3)

---

## Summary

Popliteal cyst, also called Baker cyst, is a <u>synovial fluid</u>-filled distention of a <u>bursa</u> in the <u>popliteal fossa</u>. It can be <u>idiopathic</u> or associated with underlying conditions, e.g., <u>meniscal tear</u> or <u>osteoarthritis</u>. Popliteal cysts are often discovered incidentally on imaging or <u>physical examination</u> but can also cause <u>posterior</u> <u>knee pain</u> and/or limit knee <u>flexion</u>. Large or ruptured cysts can cause calf swelling and may mimic the signs and symptoms of <u>DVT</u>. The diagnosis is usually clinical, but <u>ultrasound</u> is often used to exclude <u>DVT</u> and confirm the diagnosis. <u>X-ray</u> and/or <u>MRI</u> can be obtained to assess for underlying <u>joint</u> disease. Management of symptomatic cysts typically involves a trial of nonsurgical measures, e.g., <u>pain management</u> with <u>NSAIDs</u> and cyst drainage. Surgical resection may be considered for complications such as neurovascular compression or for persistent symptomatic cysts.

---

## Definitions

* A <u>synovial fluid</u>-filled distention of a <u>bursa</u> in the <u>popliteal fossa</u>, typically located between the <u>medial</u> head of the <u>gastrocnemius</u> muscle and the <u>semimembranosus muscle</u> [[2]](/library/Cw1qOQ0)

* Often communicates with the synovial space of <u>the knee joint</u>

---

## Etiology

* Inflammation of the <u>synovium</u> stimulates excessive production of <u>synovial fluid</u>. [[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

* <u>Risk factors</u>: inflammatory, degenerative, or traumatic intraarticular changes in <u>the knee joint</u> (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>osteoarthritis</u>, <u>meniscal lesions</u>)

* <u>Idiopathic</u> (primary popliteal cysts) : most common in children

---

## Clinical features

Popliteal cysts are typically asymptomatic and found incidentally on <u>physical examination</u> or imaging. [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)




* Signs

* Palpable mass in the <u>medial</u> <u>popliteal fossa</u>

* Foucher sign: Cyst is firm in full knee extension and soft in knee <u>flexion</u>.

* Possible symptoms

* <u>Posterior</u> <u>knee pain</u>, tenderness, knee <u>flexion</u> limitation

* Symptoms of the underlying pathology: e.g., <u>meniscal tear</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* Ruptured popliteal cyst: leakage of <u>synovial fluid</u> into the calf muscles  

* Calf swelling and <u>pain</u>, mimicking <u>acute compartment syndrome</u> or <u>DVT</u>

* Can cause <u>bruising</u> below the <u>medial malleolus</u> (crescent sign) [[5]](/library/HaWKNP0)





> [!TIP]
> A palpable change in cyst consistency when flexing or extending the knee differentiates popliteal cysts from other masses, which are not affected by knee position. [[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

---

## Diagnosis

* Clinical evaluation [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

* Popliteal cyst is usually a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* Perform <u>neurovascular examination</u> to rule out neurovascular compression.

* Imaging: to rule out other causes of <u>posterior</u> <u>knee pain</u> or lower limb swelling (e.g., <u>DVT</u>) [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: <u>anechoic</u> lesion

* <u>Plain x-ray</u>: <u>soft tissue</u> mass

* <u>MRI</u>: can help identify underlying <u>knee joint</u> pathology





> [!WARNING]
> Obtain an <u>ultrasound</u>, as a large or <u>ruptured popliteal cyst</u> may cause calf swelling and can mimic the signs of <u>DVT</u> (<u>pseudothrombophlebitis syndrome</u>). [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

## Treatment

* Asymptomatic cysts: : Treatment is not required in most cases. [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

* Symptomatic cysts [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

* Nonsurgical management: preferred for at least 6 weeks if there are no neurovascular complications [[4]](/library/QC1u7Q0)

* Rest, elevation, compression

* <u>Pain management</u>, e.g., with <u>NSAIDs</u> [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Treatment of underlying <u>knee joint</u> pathology

* If no improvement: Refer to orthopedics for consideration of <u>ultrasound</u>-guided drainage and/or <u>intraarticular glucocorticoid injection</u>.

* Surgical resection: for persistent symptoms and/or neurovascular compression

* <u>Ruptured popliteal cyst</u>: <u>conservative treatment</u>, e.g., <u>pain</u> relief, rest, elevation





> [!TIP]
> Consider referral to orthopedics for persistent symptomatic popliteal cyst despite <u>conservative measures</u>.

---

## Complications

* <u>Popliteal cyst rupture</u>: can cause <u>compartment syndrome</u> in rare cases

* Pseudothrombophlebitis syndrome: caused by a large or <u>ruptured popliteal cyst</u>

* Calf swelling and/or <u>pain</u>

* Positive <u>Homans sign</u>

* Cyst infection

* Neurovascular compression: e.g., <u>tibial nerve injury</u>, <u>DVT</u> due to venous compression




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
